definitions.definition: In the true sense, stainless wisdom with its retinue; conventionally, also the wisdom and treatises that lead to it — for the Vaibhāṣikas the seven canonical books, word of the Buddha arranged by disciples.
For the Sautrāntikas, not a separate basket of treatises but the sūtras in which the characteristics of dharmas are taught (e.g. the Arthaviniścaya).
An ultimate constituent that 'holds its own characteristic' (svalakṣaṇa-dhāraṇa); seventy-five kinds in five groups, existing as real entities (dravya) in all three times.
A momentary event in a series; only present dharmas exist, and many Vaibhāṣika dharmas are mere designations.

equivalents.note: Sanskrit and Pali forms of the same canonical term; school definitions differ (see the per-lineage definitions).

definitions.definition: The own-nature of a dharma, which it never gives up in any of the three times; the basis of its real existence (dravyatas).

The particular characteristic of a dharma (e.g. solidity of earth), as opposed to the general characteristics (impermanence etc.) shared by all conditioned dharmas; examined in the applications of mindfulness.
The general characteristics of conditioned dharmas — impermanent, suffering, empty, non-self — contemplated in the combined application of mindfulness.
Existing as a real entity (dravya), with its own nature; for the Vaibhāṣika, all dharmas, including those of past and future.
The Vātsīputrīyas deny that the person is dravyasat, while also denying that it is a mere designation.
Existing only as a designation over a collection (like milk over colour, smell etc., or a heap of grain); for Vasubandhu the person is such a designation over the series of aggregates.
That which exists ultimately: what does not lose its identity when broken or analysed into parts (like matter or feeling), as opposed to a pot or water.

equivalents.note: The Kośa's 'ultimately existent' vs the Pali 'ultimate'.

definitions.definition: That which exists conventionally: a thing of which the idea no longer arises when it is broken or its components are mentally removed — a pot, water.

equivalents.note: The Kośa's 'conventionally existent' vs the Pali 'convention'.

definitions.definition: With outflows: conditioned dharmas other than the path, in which the outflows adhere and grow; all such are suffering.
Without outflows: the truth of the path and the three unconditioned dharmas.
Outflow: in the Kośa's list three — of desire, of existence and of ignorance; so called because they make beings stay in saṃsāra and flow out through the six wounds of the senses.

equivalents.note: Sanskrit and Pali forms of the same canonical term; school definitions differ (see the per-lineage definitions).

definitions.definition: Conditioned: the five aggregates, produced by causes and conditions, marked by birth, duration, decay and impermanence; also called 'the times'.

equivalents.note: Sanskrit and Pali forms of the same canonical term; school definitions differ (see the per-lineage definitions).

definitions.definition: Unconditioned: space, cessation through discernment and cessation not through discernment — real, eternal, without activity.
Not real entities: space is mere absence of resistance; the cessations are mere non-arising.
Nine unconditioned dharmas are counted, including the four formless spheres and the natures of dependent origination and of the path (Vasumitra; low confidence).

equivalents.note: Sanskrit and Pali forms of the same canonical term; school definitions differ (see the per-lineage definitions).

definitions.definition: Space as an unconditioned dharma, whose nature is non-obstruction; distinct from the space-element (a cavity), which is conditioned matter.
Mere absence of tangible resistance.
Cessation through discernment: disjunction (visaṃyoga) from sāsrava dharmas, obtained separately for each bond by the wisdom that discerns the truths; it is nirvāṇa.
The non-arising of further defilement and birth once the antidote has arisen; not an entity.

equivalents.note: The Kośa identifies nirvāṇa with this cessation.

definitions.definition: Cessation not through discernment: the absolute obstruction of the arising of a dharma through the lack of its conditions.
Cessation through discernment — a real, unconditioned, eternal dharma, the disjunction from all sāsrava dharmas; the object of refuge together with the Buddha and Saṅgha.
A mere absence: the non-arising of future defilements and births; not an entity (like the extinction of a flame).
The unconditioned, the fourth of the five knowables; the relation of the person to nirvāṇa is inexpressible (low confidence).

equivalents.note: Sanskrit and Pali forms of the same canonical term; school definitions differ (see the per-lineage definitions).

definitions.definition: Aggregate, 'heap': the conditioned dharmas grouped as matter, feeling, perception, formations, consciousness; taught to those confused about mind.
The basis (āśraya) on which the person is designated; neither identical with nor different from it.

equivalents.note: Sanskrit and Pali forms of the same canonical term; school definitions differ (see the per-lineage definitions).

definitions.definition: Sense-base, 'gate of arising' of mind and mental factors: twelve (six faculties, six objects).
Element, 'lineage' (gotra): eighteen — six faculties, six objects, six consciousnesses; mind (manas) is the consciousness just past, posited to give the sixth consciousness a support.
Matter: the five sense faculties, five sense objects and unmanifest matter; what is subject to resistance and deterioration.

The four great elements — earth, water, fire, wind — with the natures of solidity, moisture, heat and motion and the functions of supporting, cohering, maturing and expanding; derived matter depends on them.

Unmanifest matter: a good or bad continuum derived from the elements, produced by manifest action or concentration, which persists even when the mind is distracted or absent; the substance of vows and non-vows.
Not a real entity; what is called avijñapti is the specific transformation of the series produced by volition.

cross_language.form: rnam par rig byed ma yin pa

definitions.definition: Manifest (informative) action: bodily vijñapti is shape (not movement, since things are momentary); vocal vijñapti is speech-sound.
Bodily action is volition that moves the body; shape is not a real entity.
Feeling, the aggregate of experience; pleasant, painful or neutral.
Perception, whose nature is the grasping of characteristics (nimitta).

equivalents.note: Sanskrit and Pali forms of the same canonical term; school definitions differ (see the per-lineage definitions).

definitions.definition: Consciousness, the bare representation (prativijñapti) of each object; six kinds; citta, manas and vijñāna have one meaning.
A root consciousness (mūlavijñāna) underlying the six is ascribed to the Mahāsāṃghikas by Asaṅga (low confidence).

equivalents.note: Sanskrit and Pali forms of the same canonical term; school definitions differ (see the per-lineage definitions).

definitions.definition: Mind, synonymous with manas and vijñāna; it always arises together with mental factors, and they share support, object, aspect, time and substance.
Mind is by nature luminous and pure, defiled only by adventitious defilements (Vasumitra).

Mental factor (caitasika), associated with mind; five classes in the Kośa (universal, universal good, universal defiled, universal bad, restricted defiled), with others undetermined — forty-six in the later count.
Class of mental factors (ten): feeling, volition, perception, desire-to-act, contact, understanding, mindfulness, attention, resolve, concentration.
Class of mental factors (ten): faith, heedfulness, tranquillity, equanimity, shame, dread of blame, non-greed, non-hatred, non-harming, vigour.
Class of mental factors (six): delusion, heedlessness, laziness, lack of faith, torpor, restlessness.
Class of mental factors (two): shamelessness, lack of dread of blame.
Class of mental factors (ten): anger, enmity, dissimulation, envy, spite, concealment, avarice, deceit, pride, harmfulness.

Formation dissociated from mind: a real conditioned dharma neither matter nor mental — possession, non-possession, homogeneity, the non-perceptual state, the two attainments, life faculty, the four characteristics, and the collections of names, phrases and syllables.
Mere designations for states of the series, not real entities.
Possession: a real dissociated force that links a dharma to a particular series (acquisition and endowment); it explains why a defilement 'belongs' to someone even when not manifest.
Not a real entity; 'possession' is the presence of an intact seed in the series.
Non-possession, the contrary force; the state of an ordinary person is non-possession of the noble path.
The state of an ordinary person: non-possession of the noble dharmas.
The series in which the noble dharmas have not arisen.

equivalents.note: The state of an ordinary person vs the ordinary person.

definitions.definition: Homogeneity: the real force of sameness by which beings belong to one class (nikāya-sabhāga).
The non-perceptual state of the non-perceiving gods: a cessation of mind and mental factors, a result of ripening.
Attainment of non-perception: entered in the fourth dhyāna by ordinary beings who mistake it for escape.
Attainment of cessation: a stopping of mind and mental factors entered from the peak of existence by noble ones for the sake of peaceful dwelling; obtained by the Buddha together with awakening.

equivalents.note: Sanskrit and Pali forms of the same canonical term; school definitions differ (see the per-lineage definitions).

definitions.definition: The life faculty, i.e. lifespan (āyus), the support of heat and consciousness.
The four characteristics of the conditioned — birth, duration, decay, impermanence — real forces that act on each dharma, themselves characterized by secondary characteristics.
Designations of the series: the conditioned comes to be having not been and ceases having been.
Collection of names; with the collections of phrases and syllables, real dissociated forces by which speech signifies; the eighty thousand dharma-aggregates are speech or name.
Cause; six kinds: efficient, co-existent, homogeneous, associated, pervasive, ripening.
Condition; four kinds: causal, immediately preceding, object and dominant conditions.
Result; five kinds: of ripening, outflow, dominance, human effort and disjunction.
Ripening: a neutral dharma counted as a being, arising from good or bad action, different in kind from its cause.
The result arises from the specific transformation of the series; ripening does not itself produce further ripening.
Faculty, 'dominant': twenty-two — six sense faculties, female, male, life, five feelings, five spiritual faculties and three pure faculties.
The desire realm: hells, ghosts, animals, humans and six classes of gods, in twenty places.
The form realm: seventeen places in four dhyāna levels.
The formless realm: no place, four by mode of birth; the mind-series rests on homogeneity and life faculty.
Destiny: five — hell-beings, ghosts, animals, humans, gods; the intermediate existence is not a destiny.
Intermediate existence between death and birth, having the form of the coming existence, seen by its own kind and the divine eye, feeding on smells.
Accepted (Kathāvatthu commentary on Kv 8.2).
Denied (Vasumitra).
Denied (Vasumitra).
A name of the intermediate being ('eater of smells'); the sūtra's gandharva present at conception is cited as scriptural proof of the intermediate existence.

equivalents.note: Sanskrit and Pali forms of the same canonical term; school definitions differ (see the per-lineage definitions).

definitions.definition: Dependent origination in twelve limbs over three lives; the Vaibhāṣikas take it as 'of states' (āvasthika), each limb being the fivefold aggregates at a stage named by what predominates.

equivalents.note: Sanskrit and Pali forms of the same canonical term; school definitions differ (see the per-lineage definitions).

definitions.definition: 'Pertaining to states': the Vaibhāṣika interpretation of dependent origination, one of four kinds (momentary, prolonged, connected, of states).
Volition, a universal mental factor; mental karma itself, from which bodily and vocal karma arise.
Mental karma includes covetousness, malice and wrong view themselves.
Action: volition and what is produced by volition (bodily and vocal action, manifest and unmanifest); the variety of the world is born of it.
Its result comes not from past karma existing now but from the specific transformation of the series it initiated.

equivalents.note: Sanskrit and Pali forms of the same canonical term; school definitions differ (see the per-lineage definitions).

definitions.definition: The ten courses of action, good and bad, the grossest actions of body, speech and mind.

equivalents.note: Sanskrit and Pali forms of the same canonical term; school definitions differ (see the per-lineage definitions).

definitions.definition: Discipline (restraint) as unmanifest matter: prātimokṣa, dhyāna-born and pure discipline; its opposite is non-discipline.

The discipline of individual liberation, eightfold by class (monk, nun, probationer, male and female novice, male and female lay follower, faster) and four in substance; given up by renouncing the training, death and other causes.
The code of 250 rules for monks and 348 for nuns recited at the poṣadha.

equivalents.note: Sanskrit and Pali forms of the same canonical term; school definitions differ (see the per-lineage definitions).

definitions.definition: The one-day-and-night fast discipline in eight limbs taken by a lay person from another in the morning until the next sunrise.
Going for refuge: to the non-learner's dharmas that make a Buddha, the learner's and non-learner's dharmas that make the Saṅgha, and to nirvāṇa.

equivalents.note: Going for refuge / the three refuges.

definitions.definition: The five deadly acts ripening immediately (in the next life) in hell: killing mother, father or an arhat, dividing the Saṅgha, wounding a Buddha.
Obstruction; three — of karma (the deadly acts), of defilement (intense defilement), of ripening (bad destinies, Kuru, non-perceiving gods).
Schism of the Saṅgha: a dissociated formation of disunion; wheel-schism (a rival teacher and path) and act-schism (separate legal acts in one boundary); its lie is the gravest sin.
One destined to Buddhahood from the time he performs the karma producing the marks; he cultivates for three incalculable aeons and a hundred aeons.
The bodhisattva passes through four conducts and ten grounds (Mahāvastu).

equivalents.note: Sanskrit and Pali forms of the same canonical term; school definitions differ (see the per-lineage definitions).

definitions.definition: Incalculable aeon; the bodhisattva's career spans three, ended respectively under Ratnaśikhin, Dīpaṅkara and Vipaśyin.
Perfection; the Kośa names the fulfilment of giving, patience, morality, vigour, meditation and wisdom in the bodhisattva career.

equivalents.note: Sanskrit and Pali forms of the same canonical term; school definitions differ (see the per-lineage definitions).

definitions.definition: Giving, whose merit is distinguished by giver, thing and field; merit arises even at a stūpa where no one receives.
A gift to the Buddha has greater fruit than a gift to the Saṅgha; offerings to stūpas bring great fruit (Vasumitra).
A gift to the Saṅgha, which includes the Buddha, has great fruit (Vasumitra).
Latent defilement, the root of existence: six (seven, ten), ninety-eight by realm and mode of abandonment; subtle, adhering, growing and binding; for the Vaibhāṣika identical with the defilement.
The defilement asleep, i.e. a seed-capacity in the series; awake it is an envelopment.
View; as a latent defilement, five: satkāya-view, view of extremes, wrong view, attachment to views, attachment to rules and observances.

equivalents.note: Sanskrit and Pali forms of the same canonical term; school definitions differ (see the per-lineage definitions).

definitions.definition: The view of the existing body: grasping 'self' and 'mine' in the aggregates.

equivalents.note: Sanskrit and Pali forms of the same canonical term; school definitions differ (see the per-lineage definitions).

definitions.definition: Perversion; four — taking the impermanent as permanent, the painful as pleasant, the impure as pure, the non-self as self.

equivalents.note: Sanskrit and Pali forms of the same canonical term; school definitions differ (see the per-lineage definitions).

definitions.definition: The doctrine that everything (the dharmas of past, present and future) exists; argued from scripture, from consciousness arising from two, from consciousness needing an existent object, and from the result of past karma.
Time-period (past, present, future); conditioned dharmas are themselves 'the times'; the times are distinguished by activity.
Activity: the capacity of a present dharma to project its result; the Vaibhāṣikas distinguish the three times by it (Vasumitra's theory of state).
Defilement; what calms them is the discernment of dharmas; a defilement arises complete from an unabandoned anuśaya, a present object and improper attention.

equivalents.note: Sanskrit and Pali forms of the same canonical term; school definitions differ (see the per-lineage definitions).

definitions.definition: Ignorance: a distinct dharma opposed to knowledge, not mere absence of knowledge; as the first limb, the past defilements; as the root, a separate outflow.

equivalents.note: Sanskrit and Pali forms of the same canonical term; school definitions differ (see the per-lineage definitions).

definitions.definition: Craving, the eighth limb of dependent origination: desire for pleasures and sexual union.

equivalents.note: Sanskrit and Pali forms of the same canonical term; school definitions differ (see the per-lineage definitions).

definitions.definition: Suffering: everything with outflows is suffering by the three kinds of suffering (of pain, of change, of conditioned existence).

equivalents.note: Sanskrit and Pali forms of the same canonical term; school definitions differ (see the per-lineage definitions).

definitions.definition: Envelopment: eight (or ten) secondary defilements — shamelessness, lack of dread of blame, envy, avarice, restlessness, remorse, torpor, sleepiness (+ anger, concealment).
The defilement awake (manifest), as opposed to its latent seed.
Secondary defilement: defiled mental factors other than the root defilements, including the envelopments and the six stains.

equivalents.note: Sanskrit and Pali forms of the same canonical term; school definitions differ (see the per-lineage definitions).

definitions.definition: Fetter: nine in the Abhidharma list; also the five lower and five higher fetters of the sūtras.
Flood: desire, existence, views, ignorance — the outflows with views separated out.
Grasping; as the ninth limb, running about to obtain pleasures; as defilement group, four kinds.
Hindrance; five, belonging to the desire realm; two are paired because they share opposite, nutriment and function.
To be abandoned by seeing: the anuśayas cut by the vision of the four truths (88 of the 98).
To be abandoned by cultivation: the anuśayas cut on the path of cultivation (10 of the 98), in nine grades per plane.
The path of seeing: pure, fifteen moments of acceptance and knowledge regarding the four truths, seeing what was not seen before.
The path of cultivation: mundane or pure, abandoning the defilements abandoned by cultivation grade by grade.
The path of the non-learner, the arhat, after the knowledge of destruction.
The four noble lineages: contentment with robes, alms-food and lodging, and delight in abandonment and cultivation — antidotes to craving.
Contemplation of the unlovely (skeleton contemplation), entry to cultivation for those dominated by passion; it is non-greed.
Mindfulness of breathing, entry to cultivation for those dominated by discursive thought; it is wisdom, with wind as object, in six phases (counting etc.).

equivalents.note: Sanskrit and Pali forms of the same canonical term; school definitions differ (see the per-lineage definitions).

definitions.definition: Application of mindfulness to body, feeling, mind and dharmas, by their particular and general characteristics; in substance wisdom.

cross_language.form: dran pa nye bar gzhag pa

equivalents.note: Sanskrit and Pali forms of the same canonical term; school definitions differ (see the per-lineage definitions).

definitions.definition: The four roots of good conducive to penetration — heat, summits, acceptance, highest worldly dharmas — born of cultivation.
The first root of penetration, with the four truths in sixteen aspects as object — the sign that the fire of the noble path is near.
The second root of penetration; one who obtains it never cuts the roots of good.
Acceptance: the third root of penetration (one who obtains it never goes to bad destinies); also the pure acceptances of the path of seeing, uninterrupted paths.
The fourth root of penetration, lasting one moment, immediately followed by the path of seeing.
Good conducive to liberation, planted before the roots of penetration; liberation then comes in three lives at the quickest.
Dharma-knowledge: pure knowledge of the truths regarding the desire realm.
Subsequent knowledge: pure knowledge of the truths regarding the upper realms.
Knowledge of destruction (of the outflows), arising when the vajra-like concentration has done its work; with the knowledge of non-arising, it is awakening.
Knowledge of non-arising, possessed by the unshakeable arhat: 'what was to be known is known; it will not be known again'.
Follower through faith: one of weak faculties on the path of seeing.

equivalents.note: Sanskrit and Pali forms of the same canonical term; school definitions differ (see the per-lineage definitions).

definitions.definition: Follower through dharma: one of sharp faculties on the path of seeing.

equivalents.note: Sanskrit and Pali forms of the same canonical term; school definitions differ (see the per-lineage definitions).

definitions.definition: Stream-enterer: one in the first fruit from the sixteenth moment; 'seven times at most'; for the Sarvāstivāda cannot fall back from the fruit.

equivalents.note: Sanskrit and Pali forms of the same canonical term; school definitions differ (see the per-lineage definitions).

definitions.definition: Once-returner: one who has abandoned six of the nine grades of desire-realm defilement.

equivalents.note: Sanskrit and Pali forms of the same canonical term; school definitions differ (see the per-lineage definitions).

definitions.definition: Non-returner: one who has abandoned all nine grades; reaches nirvāṇa in the intermediate state, on arising, with or without effort, or going upward.

equivalents.note: Sanskrit and Pali forms of the same canonical term; school definitions differ (see the per-lineage definitions).

definitions.definition: Arhat: the non-learner after the knowledge of destruction; six kinds, five of which can fall back (Sarvāstivāda).
The arhat does not fall back from arhatship.

Per the Sarvāstivāda reports, the Mahāsāṃghika side accepted Mahādeva's five points: an arhat may be tempted by others, has non-knowing and doubt, is instructed by others; yet arhats do not fall back (Vasumitra).

equivalents.note: Sanskrit and Pali forms of the same canonical term; school definitions differ (see the per-lineage definitions).

definitions.definition: The diamond-like concentration: the uninterrupted path of the ninth grade at the peak of existence, which destroys the last defilement.
Falling back: from what is obtained, what is not obtained, or enjoyment; possible for five of the six kinds of arhat, not from stream-entry; one fallen does not die before regaining the fruit.
No falling back from arhatship, since defilements abandoned by seeing do not return.
Stream-enterers can fall back, arhats cannot (Vasumitra).
The thirty-seven wings of awakening, ten in substance (faith, vigour, mindfulness, wisdom, concentration, joy, equanimity, tranquillity, morality, intention).

equivalents.note: Sanskrit and Pali forms of the same canonical term; school definitions differ (see the per-lineage definitions).

definitions.definition: Faith by understanding in the Buddha, Dharma, Saṅgha and morality, obtained on the path of seeing.

equivalents.note: Sanskrit and Pali forms of the same canonical term; school definitions differ (see the per-lineage definitions).

definitions.definition: The eighteen qualities exclusive to a Buddha: ten powers, four confidences, three applications of mindfulness, great compassion.
Great compassion, one of the Buddha's exclusive qualities: a conventional knowledge differing from ordinary compassion in eight ways.

Superknowledge; six — magical power, divine ear, knowledge of others' minds, recollection of former lives, knowledge of death and rebirth, destruction of outflows; the last three are the 'knowledges' (vidyā).

equivalents.note: Sanskrit and Pali forms of the same canonical term; school definitions differ (see the per-lineage definitions).

definitions.definition: Magical power: in substance concentration; movement and creation; arising from cultivation, birth, spells, herbs or karma.

equivalents.note: Sanskrit and Pali forms of the same canonical term; school definitions differ (see the per-lineage definitions).

definitions.definition: Meditative absorption, four, both as births (heavens) and as attainments; the attainment is good one-pointedness with its accompaniment; each has its factors.

equivalents.note: Sanskrit and Pali forms of the same canonical term; school definitions differ (see the per-lineage definitions).

definitions.definition: Attainment: the eight fundamental attainments (four dhyānas, four formless), each tasting, pure or pure-of-outflows; also the attainments of non-perception and cessation.
Immeasurable; four — loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, equanimity — antidotes to malice etc., with beings of the desire realm as object.

equivalents.note: Sanskrit and Pali forms of the same canonical term; school definitions differ (see the per-lineage definitions).

definitions.definition: Loving-kindness, the first immeasurable, in substance non-hatred, with the aspect 'may beings be happy'.

equivalents.note: Sanskrit and Pali forms of the same canonical term; school definitions differ (see the per-lineage definitions).

definitions.definition: Deliverance; eight — two of the unlovely, one of the beautiful, four formless, and cessation.
Totality; ten — eight (earth, water, fire, wind, blue, yellow, red, white) in the fourth dhyāna, two (space, consciousness) formless.

equivalents.note: Sanskrit and Pali forms of the same canonical term; school definitions differ (see the per-lineage definitions).

definitions.definition: The true Dharma, twofold: scripture (āgama) and realization (adhigama), upheld by teachers and practitioners; at its last breath in a time of strong stains.
In Buddhist usage: the transmitted scripture (the sūtra collections — Dīrgha, Madhyama, Saṃyukta, Ekottarika); one of the two aspects of the true Dharma.

notes: Buddhist sense only; the Śaiva/Pāñcarātra Āgamas are other units' definitions.

definitions.definition: Realization, the Dharma as attained (the wings of awakening), the second aspect of the true Dharma.
A follower of the Vibhāṣā — those who 'live by' or 'know' the Vibhāṣā; the Kashmiri orthodoxy whose system the Kośa mostly presents.
One who takes the sūtras, not the treatises, as authority (Yaśomitra).
The teaching of those who distinguish: some of the past exists (unripened karma) and some does not.
Seed: the name-and-form in a series capable of producing a result directly or mediately through the specific transformation of the series; latent defilements are such seeds.
The specific transformation of the series: the process by which a seed matures into its result without any past entity persisting — as a lac-dyed citron flower yields red pulp.
Series, continuum of momentary dharmas that is conventionally called a person; the self is a designation for it.
Momentariness: the conditioned is momentary, perishing as soon as it arises (the reason bodily manifestation is shape, not movement).
Destruction has no cause: what arises perishes of itself.
Some formations are momentary, others endure for a time (Vasumitra).
The person: real, neither the same as the aggregates nor different from them, designated in dependence on the present appropriated aggregates as fire on fuel; the fifth, inexpressible knowable.
A mere designation over the series of aggregates; there is no self (AK 3.18).
Not known as a real and ultimate fact (Kathāvatthu 1.1).

equivalents.note: Sanskrit and Pali forms of the same canonical term; school definitions differ (see the per-lineage definitions).

definitions.definition: Inexpressible: the status of the person, which cannot be stated as other than or the same as the aggregates; a fifth category of knowables.
Designation in dependence: the person is designated taking the aggregates as basis, as fire taking fuel.
The bearer of the burden (Bhārahāra-sūtra), read as the person distinct from the burden of the aggregates.
The earlier aggregates, which harm the later, are spoken of as the bearer.
Supramundane: the Buddha's conduct, roots of merit, postures, body, robes and food are beyond the world.
All Tathāgatas are supramundane and without outflows (Vasumitra).
In the Kośa, 'supramundane' qualifies the pure path (e.g. detachment by the supramundane path), not the Buddha's body.

equivalents.note: Sanskrit and Pali forms of the same canonical term; school definitions differ (see the per-lineage definitions).

definitions.definition: Conformity to the world: the Buddhas wash, eat, drink, take medicine and show age while free of dirt, hunger, thirst, illness and ageing.
Ground of the bodhisattva; ten in the Mahāvastu, from Hard to Enter to Consecration.
Plane (of existence or of meditation): the nine planes — desire realm, four dhyānas, four formless — in which defilements are abandoned grade by grade.
Conduct of the bodhisattva; four — natural, of the vow, conforming, not turning back.
The vow to become a Buddha, first made by Śākyamuni before a former Buddha Śākyamuni; the second of the four conducts.
Mind luminous by nature, defiled by adventitious defilements (Vasumitra).
Attributed to the Vibhajyavādins and rejected by the Vibhāṣā.

equivalents.note: The Mahāsāṃghika 'naturally luminous mind' and the Pali 'luminous mind' (AN 1.51–52) — the schools read the luminosity differently.

definitions.definition: A root consciousness, reported by Asaṅga as the Mahāsāṃghika name for what the Yogācāra calls the storehouse consciousness.

equivalents.note: Asaṅga's own identification (Mahāyānasaṃgraha 1); the Mahāsāṃghika texts themselves are lost

definitions.definition: A question to be set aside, the fourth way of answering (e.g. whether one who has died arises, whether the self is other than the aggregates).
The central mountain, made of four jewels, rising 80,000 leagues above the water and sunk as deep, ringed by seven golden ranges and the continents; on its summit the Thirty-Three gods.
Aeon: of destruction, formation, intermediate (from immeasurable lifespan to ten years and back), and great (eighty intermediate aeons).

equivalents.note: Sanskrit and Pali forms of the same canonical term; school definitions differ (see the per-lineage definitions).

definitions.definition: Defeat: the four gravest offences for a monk (sexual intercourse, taking what is not given, killing a human, falsely claiming superhuman states), entailing loss of monkhood.

notes: The same category occurs in every surviving Vinaya (Dharmaguptaka, Mahīśāsaka, Mahāsāṃghika, Sarvāstivāda, Mūlasarvāstivāda, Pali); the definition is given once under the Dharmaguptaka code, the living East Asian one.

definitions.definition: Offences (thirteen) requiring a formal act of the Saṅgha — probation and penance — for rehabilitation.

notes: The same category occurs in every surviving Vinaya (Dharmaguptaka, Mahīśāsaka, Mahāsāṃghika, Sarvāstivāda, Mūlasarvāstivāda, Pali); the definition is given once under the Dharmaguptaka code, the living East Asian one.

definitions.definition: The two 'undetermined' offences, judged by the testimony of a trustworthy laywoman.

notes: The same category occurs in every surviving Vinaya (Dharmaguptaka, Mahīśāsaka, Mahāsāṃghika, Sarvāstivāda, Mūlasarvāstivāda, Pali); the definition is given once under the Dharmaguptaka code, the living East Asian one.

definitions.definition: Thirty offences involving forfeiture of an improperly obtained article, followed by confession.

notes: The same category occurs in every surviving Vinaya (Dharmaguptaka, Mahīśāsaka, Mahāsāṃghika, Sarvāstivāda, Mūlasarvāstivāda, Pali); the definition is given once under the Dharmaguptaka code, the living East Asian one.

definitions.definition: Offences requiring confession (90 in the Dharmaguptaka and Sarvāstivāda codes, 92 in the Pali and Mahāsāṃghika).

notes: The same category occurs in every surviving Vinaya (Dharmaguptaka, Mahīśāsaka, Mahāsāṃghika, Sarvāstivāda, Mūlasarvāstivāda, Pali); the definition is given once under the Dharmaguptaka code, the living East Asian one.

definitions.definition: Four offences to be acknowledged, concerning food.

notes: The same category occurs in every surviving Vinaya (Dharmaguptaka, Mahīśāsaka, Mahāsāṃghika, Sarvāstivāda, Mūlasarvāstivāda, Pali); the definition is given once under the Dharmaguptaka code, the living East Asian one.

definitions.definition: Rules of training on deportment (numbers differ most between the codes: 75 Pali, 100 Dharmaguptaka, 66 Mahāsāṃghika, 113 Sarvāstivāda).

notes: The same category occurs in every surviving Vinaya (Dharmaguptaka, Mahīśāsaka, Mahāsāṃghika, Sarvāstivāda, Mūlasarvāstivāda, Pali); the definition is given once under the Dharmaguptaka code, the living East Asian one.

definitions.definition: Seven procedures for settling disputes.

notes: The same category occurs in every surviving Vinaya (Dharmaguptaka, Mahīśāsaka, Mahāsāṃghika, Sarvāstivāda, Mūlasarvāstivāda, Pali); the definition is given once under the Dharmaguptaka code, the living East Asian one.

definitions.definition: Full ordination as bhikṣu or bhikṣuṇī by a formal act of motion and three proclamations before a quorum (ten, or five in border lands).

notes: The same category occurs in every surviving Vinaya (Dharmaguptaka, Mahīśāsaka, Mahāsāṃghika, Sarvāstivāda, Mūlasarvāstivāda, Pali); the definition is given once under the Dharmaguptaka code, the living East Asian one.

definitions.definition: Going forth: novice ordination with the ten precepts.

notes: The same category occurs in every surviving Vinaya (Dharmaguptaka, Mahīśāsaka, Mahāsāṃghika, Sarvāstivāda, Mūlasarvāstivāda, Pali); the definition is given once under the Dharmaguptaka code, the living East Asian one.

equivalents.note: Sanskrit and Pali forms of the same canonical term; school definitions differ (see the per-lineage definitions).

definitions.definition: The fortnightly observance at which the monastic community of a boundary gathers, confesses and recites the prātimokṣa.

notes: The same category occurs in every surviving Vinaya (Dharmaguptaka, Mahīśāsaka, Mahāsāṃghika, Sarvāstivāda, Mūlasarvāstivāda, Pali); the definition is given once under the Dharmaguptaka code, the living East Asian one.

definitions.definition: The 'invitation' at the end of the rains, where each monastic invites correction for what was seen, heard or suspected.

notes: The same category occurs in every surviving Vinaya (Dharmaguptaka, Mahīśāsaka, Mahāsāṃghika, Sarvāstivāda, Mūlasarvāstivāda, Pali); the definition is given once under the Dharmaguptaka code, the living East Asian one.

definitions.definition: The three-month rains retreat.

notes: The same category occurs in every surviving Vinaya (Dharmaguptaka, Mahīśāsaka, Mahāsāṃghika, Sarvāstivāda, Mūlasarvāstivāda, Pali); the definition is given once under the Dharmaguptaka code, the living East Asian one.

definitions.definition: The robe-making ceremony after the rains with its privileges.

notes: The same category occurs in every surviving Vinaya (Dharmaguptaka, Mahīśāsaka, Mahāsāṃghika, Sarvāstivāda, Mūlasarvāstivāda, Pali); the definition is given once under the Dharmaguptaka code, the living East Asian one.

definitions.definition: The formula of a legal act of the Saṅgha (motion and proclamations).

notes: The same category occurs in every surviving Vinaya (Dharmaguptaka, Mahīśāsaka, Mahāsāṃghika, Sarvāstivāda, Mūlasarvāstivāda, Pali); the definition is given once under the Dharmaguptaka code, the living East Asian one.

definitions.definition: The ritually established boundary within which a Saṅgha performs its acts together; a wheel-schism cannot occur where no boundary is fixed.

notes: The same category occurs in every surviving Vinaya (Dharmaguptaka, Mahīśāsaka, Mahāsāṃghika, Sarvāstivāda, Mūlasarvāstivāda, Pali); the definition is given once under the Dharmaguptaka code, the living East Asian one.

definitions.definition: The eight weighty rules accepted by nuns, subordinating the bhikṣuṇī order to the bhikṣu order in formal matters.

notes: The same category occurs in every surviving Vinaya (Dharmaguptaka, Mahīśāsaka, Mahāsāṃghika, Sarvāstivāda, Mūlasarvāstivāda, Pali); the definition is given once under the Dharmaguptaka code, the living East Asian one.

equivalents.note: Sanskrit and Pali forms of the same canonical term; school definitions differ (see the per-lineage definitions).

definitions.definition: Probationer: a female novice in a two-year training before full ordination.

notes: The same category occurs in every surviving Vinaya (Dharmaguptaka, Mahīśāsaka, Mahāsāṃghika, Sarvāstivāda, Mūlasarvāstivāda, Pali); the definition is given once under the Dharmaguptaka code, the living East Asian one.

definitions.definition: Ascetic practices (twelve or thirteen in the lists): wearing rag-robes, three robes only, alms-round, one meal, living in the forest, at the root of a tree, in the open, in a charnel ground, sitting without lying down, and others.

notes: The same category occurs in every surviving Vinaya (Dharmaguptaka, Mahīśāsaka, Mahāsāṃghika, Sarvāstivāda, Mūlasarvāstivāda, Pali); the definition is given once under the Dharmaguptaka code, the living East Asian one.

definitions.definition: A Buddhist 'school': a community sharing a Vinaya recitation and ordination lineage (and often doctrines); the traditions count eighteen.
A 'communal recitation' or council fixing the scriptures: the first at Rājagṛha, the second at Vaiśālī, and later councils recognized by particular schools.
Elder; as a group, the Elders who formed one side of the first schism.
Matrix, the doctrinal list from which Abhidharma analysis grew.
'Option, extensive commentary': the great commentaries on the Jñānaprasthāna, above all the Mahāvibhāṣā.
Clear realization of the truths: gradual (anupūrva), in sixteen moments.
Realization of the four truths in a single moment (ekābhisamaya) — attributed to the Mahāsāṃghika and Vibhajyavādin side in the doxographies (low confidence).
Preceptor: the senior monk (at least ten years ordained) who sponsors an ordination and under whom the new monk lives in dependence.
In the Vinaya: a teacher — the officiant of the legal act, the instructor of the candidate, or the teacher of a monk in dependence.

notes: Buddhist Vinaya sense only; other lineages' definitions of ācārya are other units'.

definitions.definition: Dependence: the relationship in which a junior monk lives under a preceptor or teacher until competent (normally five years).
